cns_cor51_rewrite.claim: Corollary~\ref{cor:CI} asserts consistency, a Gaussian limit, and nominal coverage.
cns_cor51_rewrite.what_is_wrong: (a) Step: $\hat{\theta}=\theta_0+o_p(1)$. It uses: $\sigma/\sqrt n\to0$, which the paper assumes only on: no explicit part of the printed proof. But the step applies it at: the passage from a standardized limit to unnormalized consistency. (b) Step: $\left(\hat{\theta}\pm \frac{\sigma}{n^{1/2}}\right)$. It uses: the Gaussian critical value $c_a$, which the paper assumes only on: the interval stated in the corollary. But the step applies it at: an intermediate interval with critical value $1$.
cns_cor51_rewrite.why: For the printed interval $\hat\theta\pm\sigma n^{-1/2}$ and the stated $\mathcal N(0,1)$ limit, coverage tends to $2\Phi(1)-1$ rather than $1-a$ when $c_a\ne1$.
cns_cor51_rewrite.fix: Use the fourth-moment rate to establish $\sigma/\sqrt n\to0$, and use $c_a$ with relative variance consistency in the coverage argument.

cns_b1_rewrite.claim: The printed elasticity example says an upper bound on the negative log-density derivative ensures a minimal representer.
cns_b1_rewrite.what_is_wrong: Step: For Example~\ref{ex:elasticity}. the result follows from \cite[Proposition 3 and Example 5]{ichimura2021influence}. It uses: square integrability of $-\partial_d\log f(D\mid X)$, which the paper assumes only on: no part of its stated one-sided upper bound. But the step applies it at: the claimed existence of $\eta_0^{\min}$ in $\mathbb L_2$.
cns_b1_rewrite.why: For constant $X$, $f(d)=d^{1/2}e^{-d}/\Gamma(3/2)$ on $(0,\infty)$, and $\Gamma=C_c^\infty(0,\infty)$, the score $-\partial_d\log f(d)=1-1/(2d)\leq1$ has infinite squared $L_2(f)$ norm near $0$, so the derivative functional has no $L_2$ Riesz representer on $\Gamma$.
cns_b1_rewrite.fix: Require square integrability of $-\partial_d\log f(D\mid X)$ to support its projection onto $\overline\Gamma$.
cns_b1_rewrite.gives_up: Existence from a one-sided upper bound alone.

cns_d6_rewrite.claim: The proposition asserts the displayed probability bound on $n^{1/2}|\hat\theta-\bar\theta|/\sigma$.
cns_d6_rewrite.what_is_wrong: Step: $= L^{1/2}\frac{1}{L} \sum_{\ell=1}^L \sum_{j=1}^3 \Delta_{j\ell}$. proof_edits.replacement: Since $n_\ell=n/L$, the corrected Taylor identity gives $n^{1/2}(\hat\theta-\bar\theta)=L^{1/2}L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^L(\Delta_{1\ell}+\Delta_{2\ell}+2\Delta_{3\ell})$.

On the union-bound event, $n^{1/2}|\hat\theta-\bar\theta|\leq L^{1/2}L^{-1}\sum_\ell(t_{1\ell}+t_{2\ell}+2t_{3\ell})$. For $0<\epsilon\leq1$, $\sqrt{6L/\epsilon}\leq3\sqrt L/\epsilon$ and $\sqrt{3L/\epsilon}\leq3\sqrt L/\epsilon$. Also $2t_{3\ell}=3\sqrt L\{n\mathcal R(\hat\gamma_\ell)\mathcal R(\hat\alpha_\ell)\}^{1/2}/\epsilon$. cns_lem_global_proof_note:
We extend \cite[Lemma 3.3]{chernozhukov2018global}. Write
$$
\psi_0(W)=U_1+\alpha_0^{\min}(W)U_2.
$$
By law of iterated expectations,
\begin{align*}
    \sigma^2
&=E(U_1^2)+2E\{U_1\alpha_0^{\min}(W)U_2\}+ E(\{\alpha_0^{\min}(W)U_2\}^2) \\
&=E\{E(U_1^2 \mid W)\}+2E\{U_1\alpha_0^{\min}(W) E(U_2 \mid W)\}+ E\{\alpha_0^{\min}(W)^2 E(U_2^2 \mid W)\}.
\end{align*} Retain the covariance term. Put $A=\|\alpha_0^{\min}\|_2$. The conditional second-moment bounds give $\tilde cA\leq\|\alpha_0^{\min}U_2\|_2\leq\bar cA$, while $\|U_1\|_2\leq\bar c$. Reverse Minkowski gives $\sigma=\|U_1+\alpha_0^{\min}U_2\|_2\geq[\tilde cA-\bar c]_+$; Minkowski gives $\sigma\leq\bar c(1+A)$. These inequalities retain any covariance between the two score terms.
$$ By Minkowski and conditional expectation, for $q=3,4$,
\begin{align*}
\|\psi_0\|_{\text{\normalfont pr},q}&\leq\|U_1\|_{\text{\normalfont pr},q}+\|\alpha_0^{\min}(W)U_2\|_{\text{\normalfont pr},q}\\
&=\|U_1\|_{\text{\normalfont pr},q}+\left[E\{|\alpha_0^{\min}(W)|^qE(|U_2|^q\mid W)\}\right]^{1/q}\\
&\leq\bar c+\bar c\|\alpha_0^{\min}\|_{\text{\normalfont pr},q}\leq\bar c\{1+c(A^2\vee1)\}.
\end{align*}
\end{align*}

cns_cont_deriv.printed:
\label{lemma:cont}
Suppose the weighting is bounded,  namely $\ell_h \leq C<\infty$, and $\Gamma\subset \mathbb{L}_2$. The following conditions are sufficient for $\bar{Q}<\infty$ with $q=1$ in Examples~\ref{ex:CATE} and~\ref{ex:RDD}, and for $\bar{Q}<\infty$ with $q=1/2$ in Examples~\ref{ex:elasticity} and~\ref{ex:deriv}.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Example~\ref{ex:CATE}. $\pi_0(v,x)$ is bounded away from zero and one.
    \item Example~\ref{ex:RDD}. The bandwidth is fixed.
    \item Example~\ref{ex:elasticity}. $f(d\mid x)$ vanishes for each $d$ in the boundary of the support of $D$ given $X=x$ almost everywhere. $-\partial_d \log f(d \mid x)$ is a bounded above, and $\Gamma$ consists of functions
    $\gamma$ that are twice continuously differentiable in the first argument and that satisfy $E[ \{\partial_d \gamma(D,X)\}^2]<\infty$ and $E[ \{\partial^2_d \gamma(D,X)\}^2]<\infty$.
     \item Example~\ref{ex:deriv}. $f(d\mid v,x)$ vanishes for each $d$ in the boundary of the support of $D$ given $(V,X)=(v,x)$ almost everywhere. $-\partial_d \log f(d \mid v,x)$ is a bounded above, and $\Gamma$ consists of functions
    $\gamma$ that are twice continuously differentiable in the first argument and that satisfy $E[ \{\partial_d \gamma(D,V,X)\}^2]<\infty$ and $E[ \{\partial^2_d \gamma(D,V,X)\}^2]<\infty$.
\end{enumerate} [Hypotheses: ass:cont-weighting-and-space, ass:cont-space, ass:cont-deriv-boundary, ass:cont-deriv-score-and-class]

cns_brr_local_alt3.printed:
\label{lemma:bounded_RR_local}
Suppose $\alpha_0^{\min}$ exists and $\Gamma\subset \mathbb{L}_2$. Further suppose there exist $(\tilde{f}, \bar f, \bar f', h_0,\bar{K})$ bounded away from zero and above such that the following conditions hold.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Valid neighborhood. There exists $N_{h_0}(v)=(v':|v'-v|\leq h)\subset \mathcal{V}$.
    \item Bounded density. The density $f_V$ obeys, for all $v'$ in $N_{h_0}(v)$,
    $$
  0< \tilde{f} \leq f_V(v') \leq \bar f,\quad |\partial f_V(v')| \leq \bar f'.
    $$
    \item Bounded kernel. $|K(u)|\leq \bar{K}$.
    \item The conditions of Lemma~\ref{lemma:bounded_RR_global} hold, allowing bandwidth to vanish.
\end{enumerate}
Then the finite sample bound in the proof holds. In summary,
$$
\bar{\alpha}_h\lesssim h^{-1}\rightarrow \infty.
$$ [Hypotheses: ass:bounded-local-representer-exists, ass:bounded-local-space, ass:bounded-local-constants, ass:bounded-local-neighborhood, ass:bounded-local-density, ass:bounded-local-kernel, ass:bounded-local-global-conditions, ass:brr-global-setup, ass:brr-global-space, ass:brr-global-elasticity-bound]
cns_brr_local_alt3.corrected:
\label{lemma:bounded_RR_local}
Suppose $\alpha_0^{\min}$ exists and $\Gamma\subset\mathbb{L}_2$. Further suppose there exist $(\tilde f,\bar f,\bar f',h_0,\bar K)$ bounded away from zero and above such that the following conditions hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Valid neighborhood. There exists $N_{h_0}(v)=\{v':|v'-v|\leq h_0\}\subset\mathcal V$.
\item Bounded density. The density $f_V$ obeys, for all $v'$ in $N_{h_0}(v)$,
$$0<\tilde f\leq f_V(v')\leq\bar f,\quad|\partial f_V(v')|\leq\bar f'.$$
\item Bounded kernel. $|K(u)|\leq\bar K$.
\item The conditions of Lemma~\ref{lemma:bounded_RR_global} hold, allowing bandwidth to vanish. For Example~\ref{ex:elasticity}, $\alpha_0^{\min}$ that solves $-\partial_d\log f(d\mid x)=E\{\alpha(X,Z)\mid D=d,X=x\}$ is bounded above.
\end{enumerate}
Suppose in addition that $\partial_d\ell_h(V)=0$ almost everywhere, $\|\alpha_0^{\min}\|_\infty\leq\check\alpha<\infty$, and $c_\omega=\inf_{0<h<h_0}|\omega_h|>0$. Then the finite sample bound
$$\|\alpha_0^{\min,h}\|_\infty\leq\frac{\check\alpha\bar K}{c_\omega h}$$
holds. In summary,
$$\bar\alpha_h\lesssim h^{-1}\rightarrow\infty.$$

proof_edits.original: From the classic result \citep{lehmann1999elements}, we have $$ \sqrt{N_t} (\widehat{\sigma}_t^2 - \sigma_t^2) \stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{N} \left\{ 0, \text{var}(Y_t - \mu_t)^2 = \sigma^4 ( \kappa_t - 1 ) \right\}, $$ and therefore using delta-method we have that $$ \sqrt{N_t} (\log \widehat{\sigma}_t^2 - \log \sigma_t^2) \stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{N}(0, \kappa_t - 1 ). $$
proof_edits.replacement: Under the independent sampling and complete randomization condition, conditional on the assignment the observations in arm $t$ are independent draws from $Y(t)$. Write $Q_t=(Y(t)-\mu_t)^2$. Since $E(Q_t)=\sigma_t^2$ and $\operatorname{var}(Q_t)=E\{(Y(t)-\mu_t)^4\}-\sigma_t^4=\sigma_t^4(\kappa_t-1)$, the finite fourth moment and the central limit theorem give $\sqrt{N_t}\{N_t^{-1}\sum Q_{ti}-\sigma_t^2\}\stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{N}\{0,\sigma_t^4(\kappa_t-1)\}$. The difference between $\widehat{\sigma}_t^2$ and $N_t^{-1}\sum Q_{ti}$ is $O_P(N_t^{-1})$, because $\widehat{\\mu}_t-\mu_t=O_P(N_t^{-1/2})$; hence the same limit holds for $\widehat{\sigma}_t^2$. Since $\sigma_t^2>0$, the delta method, with derivative $1/\sigma_t^2$, yields $\sqrt{N_t}(\log\widehat{\sigma}_t^2-\log\sigma_t^2)\stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{N}(0,\kappa_t-1)$.

insert_after.text: Conditional on any assignment of the fixed group sizes, the two observed arm samples involve disjoint independent potential-outcome pairs, so the two log-variance limits are independent; their unconditional joint law is the same. Put $V_N=(\kappa_1-1)/N_1+(\kappa_0-1)/N_0$. Continuity and nondegeneracy imply $\kappa_t>1$: equality in $E(Q_t^2)\geq E(Q_t)^2$ would make $|Y(t)-\mu_t|$ constant almost surely. Thus $V_N>0$. Since $N_1/N\rightarrow r\in(0,1)$, both group sizes diverge and the independent weighted normal limits give $(\log\widehat{\sigma}_1^2-\log\widehat{\sigma}_0^2)/\sqrt{V_N}\stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ under $\sigma_1^2=\sigma_0^2$.

The law of large numbers for the sample second and fourth central moments gives $\widehat{\kappa}_t\rightarrow\kappa_t$ in probability. Because $N_1/N$ has an interior limit and $\kappa_1+\kappa_0>2$, the ratio of the estimated denominator squared to $V_N$ converges in probability to $1$. Each sample variance is positive with probability tending to $1$, and the estimated denominator is positive with probability tending to $1$; assigning $t_{kvar}=0$ on the complementary event therefore does not change the limit.

dfm_sks.printed:
{}
Let $r = \lim_{N\rightarrow \infty}N_1/N$, $BB(\cdot)$ be a standard Brownian Bridge, and $\xi(\cdot)$ be a Gaussian Process with mean function $0$ and covariance function 
$
\text{cov}\{ \xi(x), \xi(y) \}  =  \sigma_0^2 f_0(x)f_0(y).
$ 
The limiting distribution of the SKS statistic is
$$
\sqrt{N}t_{SKS} = \sup_y\Big | \sqrt{N} \left\{     \widehat{F}_1( y+\widehat{\tau} ) - \widehat{F}_0(y)  \right\}  \Big|
 \stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow} \sup_y \Big |   \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}} SBB_1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-r}} SBB_0  \Big|,
$$
 where $SBB_1(\cdot)$ and $SBB_0(\cdot)$ are independent realizations of the \textit{shifted Brownian Bridge} processes:
 $
 SBB(\cdot) \equiv BB(\cdot) + \xi(\cdot),
 $
 with covariance structure 
\[ 
\text{cov}\{ BB(x), \xi(y) \}= f_0(y) F_0(x)\{ 1\!-\! F_0(x) \}  \left[   E\{ Y(0) \mid Y(0)\leq x\} -  E\{ Y(0) \mid Y(0)  > x\}  \right] .
\]\label{thm::sks-nuisance} [Hypotheses: ass:constant-shift-null]
dfm_sks.corrected:
Suppose the potential-outcome pairs are independent draws from a common joint distribution with continuous, nondegenerate marginals, and that, independently of those draws, a complete randomization assigns exactly $N_1$ units to treatment and $N_0$ to control, with $N_1/N\rightarrow r\in(0,1)$. Suppose in addition that $F_0$ has a bounded uniformly continuous density $f_0$ and $E\{Y(0)^2\}<\infty$. Let $r=\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}N_1/N$, $BB(\cdot)$ be a standard Brownian Bridge on $[0,1]$, and $\xi(\cdot)$ be a Gaussian Process, jointly Gaussian with $BB\{F_0(\cdot)\}$, with mean function $0$ and covariance function
$
\text{cov}\{\xi(x),\xi(y)\}=\sigma_0^2f_0(x)f_0(y).
$
The limiting distribution of the SKS statistic is
$$
\sqrt{N}t_{SKS}=\sup_y\Big|\sqrt{N}\left\{\widehat{F}_1(y+\widehat{\tau})-\widehat{F}_0(y)\right\}\Big|
\stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow}\sup_y\Big|\frac{1}{\sqrt r}SBB_1(y)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-r}}SBB_0(y)\Big|,
$$
where the supremum is over $y\in\mathbb{R}$ and $SBB_1(\cdot)$ and $SBB_0(\cdot)$ are independent realizations of the \textit{shifted Brownian Bridge} process
$
SBB(y)\equiv BB\{F_0(y)\}+\xi(y),
$
with covariance structure
\[
\text{cov}\{BB\{F_0(x)\},\xi(y)\}=f_0(y)F_0(x)\{1-F_0(x)\}\left[E\{Y(0)\mid Y(0)\leq x\}-E\{Y(0)\mid Y(0)>x\}\right].
\]\label{thm::sks-nuisance}
flat_1240_1270: Unfortunately $\tau$ is unknown in practice and is therefore a nuisance parameter.
One natural-seeming approach is to plug in the difference-in-means estimate, $\widehat{\tau} = \widehat{\mu}_1 - \widehat{\mu}_0$,  yielding the ``shifted'' KS (SKS) statistic:
Comparing this test statistic to the usual null KS distribution, however, yields invalid $p$-values.

As \cite{Babu:2004ve} note, for such tests ``the asymptotic null distribution of the test statistic may depend in a complex way on the unknown parameters.'' See also \cite[][Theorem 19.23]{van2000asymptotic}, and the relevant discussion in \cite{koenker2002inference}. We show this more formally in Theorem~\ref{thm::sks-nuisance}.

The correlation between $BB( \cdot )$ and $\xi(\cdot )$  is the ``complex dependence'' referred to above. Since the $SBB$ processes depend on $F_0(y)$, $t_{SKS}$ also depends on $F_0(y)$ and is therefore not distribution free.

In other words, Theorem~\ref{thm::sks-nuisance} demonstrates that ``naively" plugging in $\widehat{\tau}$ for $\tau$ yields a test statistic with a null distribution that is not the null distribution of the classic KS statistic.
